content:
The pen lies on the wood beside the order, angled toward my hand. Bastian Krail stands across the desk with the patience of a man who has done this a hundred times. His coat is brushed, his ledger squared against the desk's edge, his expression carrying exactly the right weight of sorrow for a burned room and a burned portrait. "It was negligence, my lord," he says. "The girl stole. The mother lost the keys. Your mother's rooms—" a small pause, pitched for grief, "—are half gone. The house requires an example, and the order is mild, I assure you. Ten lashes for the woman, the girl disciplined at her mother's side, and both turned out at month's end. Nothing excessive." Ten lashes. For a woman who carried her daughter out of a fire. I don't touch the pen. In the history I remember, someone signed something like this. In the history I remember, Elise Fen did not survive the autumn. "The physician," I say. "Neither of them has been examined." Krail's brow lifts a fraction. "This is not a matter for medicine, my lord. The offense—" "Her arm is burned. The girl's hand is burned. They've been sitting in this room for an hour." I keep my chin level. In the game, the boy in this chair would have been bored by now, or pleased. I have watched him do it. "I want Master Aldous to see them before anything is decided. That is not mercy. It is procedure. You taught me that word yourself, Master Krail—procedure before judgment." Something shifts very slightly in his stance. "Of course, my lord. After the order is signed—" "Before." I set the order aside with two fingers, deliberately, the way one moves a document one does not intend to read twice. Then I look at the prisoners. Elise Fen stands with her burned arm held against her ribs, the bandage gray and stiff, put on by someone unskilled and left too long. Her eyes are on the floor. Liora is beside her, smaller than I remember being allowed to notice, her burned palm cradled against her chest. When my gaze reaches her, she flinches—actually flinches, shoulders drawing up—and looks away. I did that. The boy I woke up as did that, over years. It's in her body already, the way a scar is. "I'm not going to lash you," I say to her. It comes out flatter than I want. I try again. "No one is. Not yet. I want to understand what happened first." "My lord." Krail's voice stays smooth, but it lowers into something coaxing. "She has confessed. What is there to understand? The keys, the entry, the lamp—" "The fire. Yes." I turn back to him. "Now the other matter. This folio." "A shipping folio, my lord. Held in my office. It was destroyed in the fire—" "It was in my mother's *locked rooms*?" "It had been sent there for storage, pending the quarterly reconciliation. A regrettable misjudgment of placement, given what occurred." A folio of shipping records, locked inside the private apartments of a dead duchess, awaiting quarterly reconciliation. That sentence does not fit together. Even at eleven, even with no memories of any other life, I don't think it would fit together. I remember the game. I remember that Krail's ledgers, years from now, were the ones Lysandra's people audited in the third route, and that by then every original page was long gone. I don't remember this folio. Nobody told an eleven-year-old about folios. But I know what a man sounds like when he has rehearsed an answer, because I have listened to myself rehearse excuses. "Show me the entry," I say. "In the estate register." "The register was damaged—" "It was damaged. Not burned." The register is on the side table now, actually; it was carried here with the portrait's salvage, its edge charred, its stitching intact. I pull it toward me. "The register records what enters my mother's wing. If a folio was sent there for storage, someone logged it. That is also procedure." For the first time, Krail is silent for a full two seconds. "Entries of that kind are made by the under-clerks," he says. "The page may be illegible." "Then we will wait for the under-clerks. And the physician. And a proper inventory of what survived the fire, taken before anything else in that wing is 'cleared away' by anyone." I place my hand flat on the register, over the scorch mark. "Nobody signs anything today. Nobody is punished today. Elise and Liora will be treated, fed, and kept separately—not in a cell, in the guest corridor—until I have read what's in this book." "You are delaying the house's discipline," Krail says, and now the smoothness has a thin edge under it. "Your father returns tonight, my lord. He will not thank you for leaving a theft unresolved." "Then he can resolve it when he arrives. It will still be unresolved honestly." Behind Krail, the door moves. Not much—two inches of shadow, and the pale line of a face in the gap. Magerrett has stopped pretending to pass by. Our eyes meet for a heartbeat through the opening, and she pushes the door wide and comes in without asking, the way she does everything, and closes it behind her. "I heard the register mentioned," she says, to the room at large, in a voice that dares anyone to object. "I'll sit with my brother while he reads it." Krail's jaw tightens. For a moment I think he will invoke my father directly. Then he bows—shallow, exact—and says, "As the young lord wishes. I will have the physician sent." At the door he pauses, one hand on the frame. "The folio's loss is a serious matter, Lord Nera. However it is resolved." "I know," I say. "That's why I'm reading." When he is gone, the room is very quiet. Liora is staring at me now, fear mixed with something older and more confused, as if the person in this chair has spoken in a language she half remembers. Elise has not looked up. Isolde stands at my shoulder, exactly where she has stood since the beginning, her face arranged into calm, competent reassurance that reaches her eyes and stops there. "Mage," I say quietly, "the register first. And find out who logged deliveries to my mother's wing in the last month—every name, including anyone from the estate offices." "Obviously," Magerrett says, already pulling the register toward her. Then she pauses and looks at me properly, and her eyes narrow a little, seeing something new. "When did you start talking like that?" "I woke up," I say, and turn the first page.
[Scene: West reception room, Veyrath estate, late morning of 18 September 731. Nera refused to sign Krail's punishment order, ordered medical treatment before any judgment, and challenged Krail's account of the "missing" shipping folio by invoking the partially damaged estate register, which records entries into Ilyra's wing. Krail deferred with a warning that Cassian returns tonight. Magerrett entered the room and is now reading the register with Nera; she noticed his changed manner. Krail has left to send the physician. Elise and Liora remain present, untreated so far; Liora is shaken by Nera's unfamiliar behavior. Isolde stands at Nera's shoulder. Taigar is still farther down the corridor. No punishment authorized; no confession of Krail's discovered; investigation into register entries and wing deliveries beginning.]
